observation.visible_scene: A glossy black reflective surface, lit by a soft bright gradient on the left, holds several gold Krugerrand-style coins (springbok-deer reverse on one face, Paul Kruger bust with 'SUID-AFRIKA / SOUTH AFRICA' on the other, reeded rims). Dark oval smudges beneath the coins are mirror reflections, not separate objects. At the start three coins are already airborne/settling in a loose row (left, middle, right); more coins then keep dropping from above and accumulate into a growing pile on the right-center while the leftmost coin stays comparatively isolated.
visible_changes: The initial three coins rotate and tilt as they settle: the left coin tips toward near-vertical, the middle and right coins turn to show the springbok face.
From about t=0.42s a new coin enters edge-on at the top and lands leaning on the right coin; it then flattens against the pile.
A continuous stream of additional coins falls from the top of frame throughout the excerpt, each spinning/tumbling before landing and stacking onto the existing cluster.
The pile on the right-center visibly grows in height and spread as more coins are added; coins overlap and occlude one another (deformation is occlusion, not shape change).
Late in the clip (t~3.0s onward) a large coin showing the Kruger portrait face lands prominently at the top of the pile, its bust and legend clearly readable.
The leftmost coin remains a single, mostly undisturbed coin on the left for the whole segment.
Object motion dominates; the background light gradient and reflection positions stay fixed, indicating little or no camera movement.
outside_clip_unknowns: The source or cause of the falling coins (no hand, machine, or drop origin is visible above the frame).
Whether the stream of coins continues or stops after the last frame.
The exact total number of coins involved, since several are stacked and partly hidden.
What happened to the first three coins before t=0; they are already in motion at the crop boundary.
uncertain_details: Camera motion cannot be fully confirmed; the static lighting and reflection layout suggest a fixed camera, but minor drift is not ruled out.
Distinguishing a reflection blob from an out-of-focus coin is uncertain in some frames.
The precise moment each falling coin contacts the surface is approximate due to the 12 fps sampling.
Some mid-fall coins appear as thin edge-on slivers, making their face orientation hard to read.
